title: Intervals as Shapes
intro: On the guitar every interval is a fixed fingering that works anywhere on the neck, apart from one shift at the B string. Learn the shapes from a root on strings 6 and 5 and you can build any chord or scale from its intervals.

blocks.text: Along a string the interval is just the number of frets: 1 fret = minor second, 2 = major second, 3 = minor third, 4 = major third, 5 = perfect fourth, 7 = perfect fifth, 12 = octave (see Intervals (#/arts/music-theory/intervals)).
From a root on string 6 (or 5, or 4, as long as the B string is not involved), the next string up is a perfect fourth at the same fret. Everything else follows by moving frets:

items: Next string, 2 frets back: minor third. 1 fret back: major third. Same fret: perfect fourth. 1 fret up: tritone. 2 frets up: perfect fifth.
Two strings up, 1 fret back: major sixth. Same fret: minor seventh. 1 up: major seventh. 2 up: octave.
Crossing from the G string (3) to the B string (2), every shape moves one fret higher, because that pair is a major third (4 semitones) rather than a fourth.

blocks.text: A chord is its intervals above the root (see Chords (#/arts/music-theory/chords)). Put the root on string 6, then a fifth on string 5 (+2 frets), the octave on string 4 (+2), the third on string 3 (major: +1, minor: same fret) and so on, and you have the E-shape barre chord. The A-shape barre chord is the same idea with the root on string 5. Changing one interval changes the chord: lower the third one fret for minor, lower the octave two frets to make it a dominant seventh.

blocks.title: Find the third
blocks.text: Your root is C on string 5 fret 3. Where is the major third on string 4, and the minor third?
solution: String 4 is a fourth above string 5. A major third is one semitone smaller than a fourth: one fret back, string 4 fret 2 (E). A minor third: two frets back, string 4 fret 1 (E♭).

blocks.title: Across G–B
blocks.text: Root G on string 3 fret 0 (open). Where is its perfect fifth on string 2?
solution: A perfect fifth on the next string is normally 2 frets up from the root's fret. Crossing G–B adds one fret: 3 frets up, string 2 fret 3 = D.

blocks.text: Sources: Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Tagliarino, B. (2006). Guitar Fretboard Workbook. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press.
